questions.question: How do you identify classes from a problem statement in LLD?

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to extract entities from requirements and map them to object-oriented design elements — the foundational skill of Low-Level Design.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating every noun as a class without filtering, or missing behavioral entities like managers and controllers that coordinate system operations.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that you'd also identify relationships (has-a, is-a) and potential design patterns while reading the problem statement, creating a mental dependency graph.

questions.direct_answer: Identify nouns in the problem statement — these become candidate classes. Filter to entities that have both data (attributes) and behavior (methods). Actors like managers and controllers often become classes or interfaces. Validate each class by ensuring it has clear responsibilities.

items: Nouns → candidate classes: Vehicle, ParkingSpot, Ticket, Payment
Verbs → methods on classes: park(), calculateFee(), issueTicket()
Not everything needs its own class: simple value objects can be fields
Actors (users, systems): often interfaces or abstract classes
Value objects vs entities: ParkingSpot (entity) vs Price (value object)
Group related attributes together into a class

answer_sections.content: My technique for identifying classes: I underline all the nouns in the problem statement. For a parking lot: parking lot, floor, spot, vehicle, car, motorcycle, ticket, payment, display board. These are my candidate classes. Then I filter: does it have meaningful attributes AND behaviors? ParkingSpot has attributes (spotId, type, isOccupied) and behaviors (occupy(), free(), isAvailable()) — it's a class. 'Price' might just be a BigDecimal field, not its own class. Verbs tell me what methods belong to which class: 'issue a ticket' → Ticket has an issueTicket() or the ParkingLot has issueTicket() that creates a Ticket. I also identify abstract concepts: Vehicle is abstract because the concrete types are Car and Motorcycle.

What is a value object vs an entity in domain design?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: The fastest way to find classes is grammatical: underline the nouns in the prompt, then keep only the ones with both data and behaviour.

beats.text: Identifying classes is the first step in any LLD. The trick is to read the problem statement and underline every noun — those are your candidate classes.

items: Underline nouns: parking lot, floor, spot, vehicle, car, motorcycle, ticket, payment
Filter candidates: does it have both meaningful attributes AND behaviors?
Verbs become methods: 'issue a ticket' means Ticket.issue() or ParkingLot.issueTicket()
Actors (users, external systems) often become interfaces or abstract classes
Simple values like price may just be a field — not every noun needs its own class

beats.text: ParkingSpot has attributes (spotId, type, isOccupied) and behaviors (occupy(), free(), isAvailable()) — it earns its own class. 'Price' is often just a BigDecimal field on another class, not a class by itself.
candidates miss: identifying abstract concepts. Vehicle is abstract because the concrete types are Car and Motorcycle — make that explicit early or you'll redesign later.

speakable_v2.cap: Underline nouns, filter by attributes-plus-behaviors, then check for abstract concepts. That three-step scan will get you a solid class list in two minutes.

sections.title: Identifying Classes from a Problem Statement
sections.content:
The classic technique is **noun-verb analysis**: **nouns** in the problem statement are candidate **classes**, and **verbs** are candidate **methods**. From *"a member borrows a book and pays a fine"* you get classes `Member`, `Book`, `Fine` and methods `borrow()`, `payFine()`.

Then you **filter**: keep nouns that have both **data (attributes)** and **behaviour (methods)** and a clear responsibility. Drop synonyms, vague words, and pure values. Actors like "manager" often become a class or a service. This is GeeksforGeeks-level LLD bread and butter.

sections.title: From Words to Classes
sections.content:
blue|Nouns -> Classes|~Things in the domain|Member, Book, Order|have data + behaviour|one clear responsibility
emerald|Verbs -> Methods|~Actions|borrow(), pay()|live on the owner class|the behaviour
amber|Adjectives -> Attributes|~Properties|title, price, status|fields on a class|often enums
rose|Filter out|~Not classes|synonyms, vague words|pure values (a price)|UI-only terms

sections.title: Java — Nouns Become Classes
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Turning every noun into a class** — "late", "name", "price" are attributes/values, not classes.
- **Missing actor classes** — "librarian" or "manager" often need a class or service.
- **Classes with data but no behaviour** — that's a struct; ask what it *does*.
- **Ignoring relationships** — finding classes is step one; how they connect is step two.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Nouns → classes, verbs → methods, adjectives → attributes.**
- Keep nouns with **both data and behaviour** and one clear responsibility.
- Drop synonyms, vague terms, and pure values.
- Actors (manager, librarian) become classes or services.
- Finding classes is step one — then map their relationships.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
My go-to technique is noun-verb analysis. I read the problem statement and underline the nouns, because nouns are usually the candidate classes — things like Member, Book, Order, ParkingSpot. The verbs become candidate methods, so borrow, pay, park. And adjectives or descriptive words usually become attributes, like a book's title or a spot's size.

But I don't blindly turn every noun into a class. I filter. A real class should have both data and behaviour and a single clear responsibility. So something like price is just a value — it's an attribute on a product, not its own class. A word like late is a condition, not an entity. I also watch for synonyms; if the prompt says customer in one place and user in another, that's probably one class, not two.

The one thing freshers often miss is actor classes. Words like manager, librarian, or administrator describe people who act on the system, and they frequently deserve a class or at least a service, especially when they have permissions or behaviour that differs from a regular user. Once I have my filtered list of classes, I treat that as step one and move on to the relationships — which classes contain which, which inherit from which. Identifying the classes is the foundation, but the design only takes shape once you connect them.

questions.question: What are enums useful for in LLD and how do you use them?

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of Java enums and their role in modeling domain-specific constants in Low-Level Design, including their ability to encapsulate behavior.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using String constants or integer codes instead of enums, missing the compile-time safety, IDE support, and behavioral encapsulation that enums provide.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show that enums can have fields, constructors, and methods — they're not just constant lists but full-fledged classes that can encapsulate logic specific to each constant.

questions.direct_answer: Enums represent fixed sets of constants with type safety and behavior. In LLD, use them for domain-specific categories: VehicleType with values CAR, MOTORCYCLE, TRUCK; SpotType with COMPACT, LARGE, HANDICAPPED; TicketStatus with ACTIVE, PAID, EXPIRED. They're safer and more expressive than String constants.

answer_sections.content: Enums are extremely useful in LLD for representing a fixed set of states or types. Instead of using String constants or magic integers, enums give type safety and readability. In a parking lot: VehicleType enum with CAR, MOTORCYCLE, TRUCK — now the compiler catches if I accidentally pass 'BUS' which isn't a valid type. SpotType with COMPACT, LARGE, HANDICAPPED. TicketStatus with ACTIVE, PAID, EXPIRED. Java enums can also carry data and behavior — SpotType.COMPACT can have a size field. Using enums in switch statements is clean and the compiler warns if you miss a case. They also make persistence more explicit — store the enum name as a string in the database.

follow_up_questions: How do you store an enum value in a database with JPA?
Can Java enums have abstract methods?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: Reaching for a String when you mean one of three fixed options is the bug enums were invented to delete.

beats.text: Enums represent a fixed set of constants. In LLD they replace error-prone String constants and magic integers — and the compiler enforces valid values for you.

items: VehicleType: CAR, MOTORCYCLE, TRUCK — type-safe vehicle classification
SpotType: COMPACT, LARGE, HANDICAPPED — each can carry a size field
TicketStatus: ACTIVE, PAID, EXPIRED — state machine for a ticket's lifecycle
PaymentMode: CASH, CARD, UPI — clean switch statements with compiler warnings if you miss a case

beats.text: SpotType.COMPACT can carry its own size field and a getSize() method. That's richer than a plain constant — it bundles the data and behavior that belong together.
non-obvious: Java enums can have abstract methods, meaning each constant can override the behavior differently. It's rarely needed in LLD interviews, but it shows depth if you mention it.

speakable_v2.cap: Reach for enums whenever you have a fixed set of types or states. They make your design safer, clearer, and easier to extend.

sections.title: Using Enums in LLD
sections.content:
An **enum** is a type with a **fixed set of named constants** — `VehicleType { CAR, MOTORCYCLE, TRUCK }`. In LLD they model **closed categories**: vehicle types, spot sizes, order/ticket statuses. They beat `String` or `int` constants because they're **type-safe** (the compiler rejects an invalid value) and can carry **data and behaviour**.

A Java enum can have fields, a constructor, and methods — so `SpotSize.LARGE.fits(vehicleType)` puts the logic right on the value. That's far safer than passing `"large"` strings around.

sections.title: Enums in LLD at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What enums are|~Fixed named constants|VehicleType: CAR, TRUCK|a closed set you control|not for growing lists
emerald|Type safety|~Compiler-checked|invalid values won't compile|no "Car" vs "CAR" typos|beats String/int constants
amber|Carry behaviour|~Full Java types|fields + constructor + methods|SpotSize.LARGE.fits(...)|logic on the value
rose|Common uses|~Domain categories|TicketStatus lifecycle|PaymentMode: CASH/CARD/UPI|clean switch statements

sections.title: Without enum — stringly-typed and error-prone
With enum — type-safe with behaviour
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **String/int constants** instead of enums — typos, no compiler checks, `switch` on magic numbers.
- **Enums for unbounded sets** — don't enum user-entered categories that grow; enums are for *fixed* sets.
- **Forgetting enums can have behaviour** — push logic onto the enum instead of external `switch`es.
- **Giant `switch` on an enum everywhere** — sometimes a method on the enum (or polymorphism) is cleaner.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Enums model **fixed, closed sets** of constants.
- **Type-safe**: the compiler rejects invalid values (unlike Strings).
- Java enums can hold **fields, constructors, and methods**.
- Put related logic **on the enum** (`fits`, `dailyLimit`) instead of external switches.
- Don't use enums for **unbounded/growing** categories.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
An enum represents a fixed set of named constants, and in low-level design I reach for them whenever I have a closed category — vehicle types like car, motorcycle, and truck; spot sizes like compact, regular, and large; or statuses like active, paid, and expired. The first reason is type safety. If I model vehicle type as a String, then car, Car, and CAR are all different values, typos compile fine and only blow up at runtime, and there's nothing stopping someone passing banana. With an enum, the compiler only accepts the defined values, so a whole class of bugs just disappears.

The second reason, which freshers often don't realise, is that Java enums are full-blown types. They can have fields, a constructor, and methods. So instead of writing a switch statement somewhere that maps spot size to a rank, I can give the SpotSize enum a rank field and a fits method, and then call spotSize.fits(required) directly. The behaviour lives right on the value where it belongs.

The one caveat I'd give is that enums are for fixed sets that you control. If the categories are user-defined and grow over time — like product categories an admin can add — an enum is the wrong tool, because adding a value means a code change and redeploy. For those you'd use a database table or a reference entity. But for the genuinely closed sets that dominate LLD problems, enums are safer and more expressive than strings or integers every time.

questions.question: How do you model a one-to-many relationship in LLD Java classes?

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of composition relationships and how to represent them in code using collections, along with proper encapsulation practices.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Exposing the raw List directly via a getter, allowing external code to modify the internal collection without the parent class knowing, breaking encapsulation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention defensive copying or returning unmodifiable collections using Collections.unmodifiableList or List.copyOf to prevent external modification of internal state.

questions.direct_answer: Use a collection field in the 'one' side: ParkingLot has a List of ParkingFloor objects, and ParkingFloor has a List of ParkingSpot objects. Provide controlled access methods like addFloor, removeFloor, and getFloors that return unmodifiable views to protect internal state.

answer_sections.content: One-to-many in Java classes is straightforward: the 'one' side holds a collection of the 'many'. ParkingLot has a List<ParkingFloor>. ParkingFloor has a Map<String, ParkingSpot> keyed by spot ID. The choice of collection type matters: List for ordered sequences, Set for unique items, Map for keyed lookup. I expose the relationship through methods rather than directly exposing the collection: addFloor(), getAvailableSpots(vehicleType), rather than getFloors() which exposes the internal list. This encapsulation lets me change the internal structure later — switch from List to Map for better spot lookup performance — without changing callers.

follow_up_questions: When would you use a Map instead of a List for a one-to-many relationship?
How do you handle bidirectional relationships in LLD?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: A one-to-many is just a collection field on the 'one' side — the trick is handing back an unmodifiable view, not your live list.

beats.text: A one-to-many relationship means one object owns or contains multiple instances of another. In Java, the 'one' side holds a collection field pointing to the 'many' side.

ParkingLot has a List of ParkingFloor. Each ParkingFloor has a Map keyed by spotId to ParkingSpot. The Map is better than a List here because you'll look up a spot by ID far more often than you'll iterate in order.

items: List: use when order matters or you need index access
Set: use when uniqueness matters and order doesn't
Map: use when you need fast lookup by a key — spot ID, vehicle license plate

beats.text: gotcha: don't expose the internal collection directly via a getFloors() getter. Expose it through meaningful methods like addFloor() and findAvailableSpot(). This lets you change the internal data structure later without breaking callers.

speakable_v2.cap: The 'one' side holds a collection of the 'many'. Choose List, Set, or Map based on how you'll query — and encapsulate the collection behind meaningful methods.
followup_handoff: When would you use a Map instead of a List?
How do you handle bidirectional relationships in LLD?

sections.title: Modelling One-to-Many Relationships
sections.content:
A **one-to-many** relationship is modelled with a **collection field on the "one" side**: a `ParkingLot` has a `List<ParkingFloor>`, a `ParkingFloor` has a `List<ParkingSpot>`. You add controlled mutators (`addFloor`) and a getter that returns an **unmodifiable view** so callers can't corrupt your internal list.

This is **encapsulation** applied to collections: expose the data for reading, but keep mutation behind methods that can validate. Returning the raw `List` lets any caller `clear()` it behind your back.

sections.title: One-to-Many at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|One-to-many|~Collection on the 'one'|ParkingLot has List<Floor>|Floor has List<Spot>|the one owns the many
emerald|Pick the collection|~How you'll query|List: order/index|Set: uniqueness|Map: fast lookup by key
amber|Encapsulate it|~Don't leak the list|add via addFloor()|validate on mutation|return an unmodifiable view
rose|If you leak it|~Live list = danger|callers can clear()|internal state corrupted|breaks encapsulation

sections.title: Leaky — handing out the live list
Encapsulated — controlled add + read-only view
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Returning the live `List`** — any caller can mutate your internal state.
- **No controlled add/remove** — mutation should be a method that can validate.
- **Putting the collection on the wrong side** — the *one* holds the collection of *many*.
- **Exposing setters for the whole list** — replace controlled adds, not bulk `setFloors`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- One-to-many = a **collection field on the "one" side**.
- Mutate through **controlled methods** (`addFloor`) that can validate.
- Return an **unmodifiable view** (`Collections.unmodifiableList`) from getters.
- Never hand out the **live internal list**.
- This is **encapsulation** applied to collections.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
I model a one-to-many relationship by putting a collection field on the one side. So a ParkingLot has a list of ParkingFloor objects, and each ParkingFloor has a list of ParkingSpot objects. The lot is the one, the floors are the many, and the list lives on the lot.

The part that separates a careful answer from a sloppy one is how you expose that collection. The naive approach is a getFloors method that just returns the internal list directly. The problem is that now any caller can reach in and call clear or add on your private list, and your object's internal state gets corrupted without it knowing. That breaks encapsulation.

So instead I provide controlled mutators — an addFloor method that can validate the input, reject nulls, enforce limits — and the getter returns an unmodifiable view using Collections.unmodifiableList. Callers can iterate and read all they want, but if they try to mutate the returned list, they get an exception, and they can never touch the real one. Mutation only happens through my methods, which is exactly where I can enforce invariants. It's really just encapsulation applied to collections: expose the data for reading, but keep all the changes behind methods you control. The same idea scales to many-to-many, where you'd typically introduce a join entity rather than cross-referencing lists.

questions.question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in LLD?

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of when to use inheritance versus interface contracts in object-oriented design — a core LLD decision point.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using abstract classes everywhere or not knowing Java 8+ allows default methods in interfaces, blurring the distinction.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Java allows multiple interfaces but only single inheritance, so interfaces are preferred for flexibility.

questions.direct_answer: Abstract class provides partial implementation with fields and concrete methods for IS-A relationships with shared code (Vehicle with common fields). Interface is a pure contract with no state for CAN-DO relationships (Payable, Parkable). Use interface for type hierarchy, abstract class for shared implementation.

answer_sections.content: In LLD, I use abstract class when there's a clear IS-A relationship with shared implementation. Vehicle is abstract because all vehicles share common attributes (licensePlate, size, color) and the subclasses (Car, Motorcycle) build on that. I use interfaces for capabilities or contracts that can apply to unrelated classes. Payable could apply to a Vehicle or a ParkingSubscription — they're not related by IS-A but both can be paid for. The rule: abstract class for shared code in a family of classes; interface for defining a contract that any class can implement. In modern Java, interfaces can have default methods, which blurs this a bit, but the design intent remains distinct.

follow_up_questions: Can a class extend an abstract class and implement interfaces simultaneously?
When would you change a class to an interface in a design?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: Pick abstract class when copies share code, interface when unrelated things share a capability — that one sentence decides it.

groups.heading: Abstract Class
groups.text: A partial implementation meant to be extended. Use it when related classes share code. Vehicle is abstract because Car and Motorcycle both need licensePlate, color, and size fields.

groups.heading: Interface
groups.text: A contract that defines capabilities. Use it when unrelated classes need the same behavior. Payable could apply to a Vehicle or a ParkingSubscription — they're not related by IS-A, but both can be paid for.

beats.text: Use abstract class for shared code in a family. Use interface for defining a capability that any class can implement. When in doubt, start with an interface — it's easier to loosen later than to break inheritance hierarchies.
sharp edge: Java interfaces now support default methods, which blurs the line. But the design intent still matters — don't use default methods to smuggle shared state into an interface.

speakable_v2.cap: Abstract class = shared code for an IS-A family. Interface = a contract for a CAN-DO capability. Start with interface when you're unsure.
followup_handoff: Can a class extend an abstract class and implement interfaces at the same time?
When would you refactor a class to an interface?

sections.title: Abstract Class vs Interface in LLD
sections.content:
Both define a contract, but they answer different questions. An **abstract class** models an **IS-A** relationship with **shared state and code** — `Vehicle` with common fields and a default `start()`. An **interface** is a **pure capability** (a CAN-DO) with no state — `Payable`, `Comparable`, `Parkable` — that unrelated classes can implement.

The fresher rule of thumb: use an **abstract class** when subtypes share *implementation*; use an **interface** when otherwise-unrelated classes share a *capability*. Since Java 8, interfaces can have `default` methods, but they still hold **no instance state**.

sections.title: Abstract Class vs Interface
sections.content:
blue|Abstract class|~IS-A + shared code|instance fields + state|concrete + abstract methods|single inheritance
emerald|Interface|~CAN-DO capability|no instance state|default/static methods OK|implement many
amber|Pick abstract when|~Subtypes share code|Vehicle base for Car/Truck|avoid duplicate logic|a real IS-A
rose|Pick interface when|~Unrelated share an ability|Payable, Parkable|start here if unsure|orthogonal capabilities

sections.title: Abstract Class vs Interface
sections.content:
| Aspect | Abstract Class | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| Relationship | IS-A (Car IS-A Vehicle) | CAN-DO (Car CAN-DO Parkable) |
| State (fields) | Yes — instance fields | No instance state (constants only) |
| Methods | Abstract + concrete | Abstract + `default`/`static` |
| Multiple inheritance | No (single `extends`) | Yes (`implements` many) |
| Use when | Subtypes share code | Unrelated types share a capability |
| Constructor | Yes | No |

sections.title: Wrong tool — interface forced where code is shared
Right tools — abstract class for code, interface for capability
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Abstract class = IS-A + shared code + state**; single inheritance.
- **Interface = CAN-DO capability**, no instance state; implement many.
- Use abstract class when subtypes **share implementation**.
- Use interface when **unrelated classes share a capability**.
- A class can `extends` one abstract class and `implements` several interfaces.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Both an abstract class and an interface define a contract, but they answer different questions, and that's how I decide between them. An abstract class models an is-a relationship and lets subtypes share both state and code. So Vehicle as an abstract class can hold common fields like the license plate and a concrete start method that every vehicle reuses, plus an abstract method like requiredSize that each subclass must define. The key thing is it carries implementation and instance state.

An interface is a pure capability — a can-do. Something like Parkable or Comparable says any class that implements me can do this thing, and those classes don't have to be related at all. A Car and a Bicycle might both be Parkable without sharing a base class. Interfaces hold no instance state; even with Java 8 default methods, which let you add behaviour, there are still no instance fields.

So my rule of thumb is simple: use an abstract class when your subtypes genuinely share implementation and you want to avoid duplicating it, and use an interface when otherwise-unrelated classes need to share a capability. And because Java only allows extending one class but implementing many interfaces, you often combine them — a Car extends the Vehicle abstract class for shared code and implements Parkable and maybe Insurable for orthogonal capabilities. Reaching for an interface when there's real shared code just leads to copy-pasted logic across every implementation.

questions.question: How do you define the responsibilities of each class in an LLD?

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to apply the Single Responsibility Principle in practice — assigning clear, focused responsibilities to each class without overlap or confusion.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating god classes that handle everything (ParkingLot manages spots, calculates fees, generates tickets, processes payments) or splitting responsibilities too finely into trivial classes.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that you'd validate responsibilities by asking 'what would cause this class to change?' — if there are multiple unrelated answers, the class needs splitting.

questions.direct_answer: Apply the Single Responsibility Principle: each class should have one reason to change. ParkingSpot manages spot state and availability. FeeCalculator computes parking fees based on time and vehicle type. TicketGenerator creates and validates tickets. Avoid combining unrelated behaviors in one class.

answer_sections.content: I apply the Single Responsibility Principle: each class should have one primary reason to change. In a parking lot: ParkingSpot's job is tracking whether it's occupied and what type it is — nothing about pricing. FeeCalculator calculates fees based on time and vehicle type — nothing about spots. TicketGenerator creates and manages tickets. ParkingLot coordinates the overall flow: find a spot, issue a ticket, process exit. A sign of poor SRP is a 'God class' that knows about spots, fees, tickets, and display boards. When you ask 'why would this class change?' and get three different answers, it needs to be split. Each business rule change should ideally only require changing one class.

follow_up_questions: How does SRP relate to the concept of cohesion?
What happens to your design if you violate SRP?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: The litmus test for a class's responsibility is brutal: if you can name two unrelated reasons it would change, split it.

beats.text: SRP says each class should have one primary reason to change. It's the most practical LLD principle because it directly shapes which classes you create and what goes in each.

groups.heading: ParkingSpot
groups.text: Tracks whether it's occupied and what type it is. Nothing about pricing.

groups.heading: FeeCalculator
groups.text: Calculates fees based on time and vehicle type. Nothing about spots.

groups.heading: TicketGenerator
groups.text: Creates and manages tickets. Knows entry time, spot, and vehicle.

groups.heading: ParkingLot
groups.text: Coordinates the overall flow: find a spot, issue a ticket, process exit. It delegates the details.

beats.text: production trap: the 'God class' — a ParkingLot that also calculates fees, generates tickets, and updates displays. Ask yourself: 'why would this class change?' If you get three different answers, it needs to be split.

speakable_v2.cap: Give each class one job. If you can describe a class's responsibility in one short sentence, you're on the right track.
followup_handoff: How does SRP relate to cohesion?
What happens to your design when SRP is violated?

sections.title: Defining Class Responsibilities (SRP)
sections.content:
The **Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)** says a class should have **one reason to change**. Practically: each class owns one cohesive job. `ParkingSpot` manages spot state; `FeeCalculator` computes fees; `TicketGenerator` issues tickets. Don't fuse unrelated behaviour into one class.

The test: say the class's job in one sentence with no "and". If you need "and" — *"it tracks occupancy **and** computes the bill"* — that's two responsibilities, so split it. High cohesion makes classes easy to test, reuse, and change.

sections.title: Defining Responsibilities (SRP)
sections.content:
blue|SRP|~One reason to change|one job per class|state it without 'and'|high cohesion
emerald|Split by job|~Separate concerns|ParkingSpot: occupancy|FeeCalculator: pricing|TicketPrinter: format
amber|The God class|~Anti-pattern|does everything|3 reasons to change|impossible to test
rose|Don't over-split|~The other extreme|anaemic 1-method classes|fragmented logic|aim for cohesion

sections.title: Violating SRP — one class, three jobs
Following SRP — one job each
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **The God class** — a `Manager` that does everything; impossible to test in isolation.
- **Mixing layers** — persistence + business rules + formatting in one class.
- **Confusing SRP with "one method"** — a class can have many methods serving *one* responsibility.
- **Splitting too far** — anaemic one-method classes everywhere also hurts; aim for cohesion.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **SRP**: one class, **one reason to change**.
- Test: state the job in a sentence without **"and"**.
- `ParkingSpot` (state), `FeeCalculator` (pricing), `TicketPrinter` (format) — separate jobs.
- High cohesion → easy to test, reuse, and modify.
- Avoid both the **God class** and over-fragmentation.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
I define responsibilities using the Single Responsibility Principle, which says a class should have exactly one reason to change. The practical test I use is to state the class's job in a single sentence, and if I find myself using the word and, that's a red flag. If I say ParkingSpot tracks occupancy and calculates the fee and prints the ticket, that's three responsibilities wearing one class, and each is a separate reason the class might change — occupancy rules, pricing, ticket formatting.

So I'd split that into focused classes. ParkingSpot just manages its own state — occupied or free. A FeeCalculator computes the charge. A TicketPrinter handles formatting and output. Now each class has one cohesive job, which means when pricing changes I only touch FeeCalculator, and I can unit-test it without dragging in a parking spot.

The big anti-pattern this avoids is the God class — some Manager that knows everything and is impossible to test or reason about. But I'd also caution against the opposite extreme: splitting so aggressively that you end up with dozens of anaemic one-method classes, which fragments the logic and hurts readability just as much. The target is high cohesion — everything in a class genuinely belongs together and serves the same single purpose. That balance is what makes a design both clean and practical.
